[THOUGHT]  
This case presents a classic triad highly suggestive of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD): (1) bilateral, numerous renal cysts with kidney enlargement on ultrasound; (2) early-onset hypertension (150/88 mmHg) in a patient with otherwise non-acute, insidious presentation; and (3) evidence of progressive renal dysfunction (serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL — elevated for most adults without muscle wasting or dehydration). The absence of constitutional, urinary, or GI symptoms argues against infection, malignancy, or obstruction as primary drivers. Imaging workup is appropriately directed toward characterizing cyst burden and complexity (CT, MRI), screening for extrarenal involvement (liver US), and ruling out mimics (e.g., acquired cystic kidney disease — unlikely given age and lack of ESRD history; tuberous sclerosis — no skin/neurological stigmata reported). Genetic testing for *PKD1/PKD2* is the definitive confirmatory step, especially important given that imaging criteria alone may be insufficient for diagnosis in younger patients (<30–40 years) or those with atypical cyst distribution. Family history remains pending but is pivotal: a positive family history would strongly reinforce ADPKD, while its absence does not exclude it (de novo mutations occur in ~10% of cases). Importantly, the pattern — multiple *simple*, *anechoic*, *bilateral* cysts in enlarged kidneys — is distinct from cystic neoplasms (which typically show septations, nodularity, or enhancement) or inflammatory/infectious cystic disease (which would present acutely with fever, WBC elevation, or pyuria). The clinical trajectory — slow progression over months, preserved general health, and absence of red flags — further aligns with ADPKD rather than aggressive malignancy or systemic illness.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)
